speaker: Philippe Laffont
title: He Turned  Million Into a Nearly  Billion Investment Firm | Philippe Laffont
question: In public-markets investing, why can launching a fund right into a severe market crash give a manager a long-term advantage over veterans who built their careers in a decade-long bull market?
guest: I started January first, 2000. I was up twenty percent after a month and thought it was going to be so easy, and then the NASDAQ went from 5,000 to 1,000 over three years. In retrospect, by having started in such a tough market, I was ready for anything after. All my friends, older people I met who started in the eighties or nineties, had ten or twenty years of uninterrupted success. When the bubble came, they all thought, 'Don't worry, this is just a one-time thing, it's going to go back,' and it never did. What's lucky when you start in money management at a bad time is you are not afraid to change your mind and realize that sometimes there are very important things going on in the economy—it's like a boat in a big storm, and it's time to return to port. Some people don't believe in returning to port; they just keep going. On average, there's one very bad event every ten years where the market goes down fifty percent or more, and three times a decade it goes down twenty percent or more. There's no better way to navigate choppy waters than to have started navigating choppy waters.

points.core: Long bull markets condition veteran managers to assume severe crashes are temporary dips.
points.note: Accept: prolonged bull-market success breeds complacency, expecting rapid rebounds, assuming downturns always revert quickly. Do not credit: generic claims that experience causes arrogance without tying it to crash expectations.

points.core: Starting during a crash trains managers early to de-risk when macro storms hit.
points.note: Accept: learning to return to port, changing your mind quickly, cutting exposure defensively in downturns. Do not credit: vague advice to manage risk or stay disciplined.

points.core: Major market drawdowns recur predictably every decade, punishing funds that never play defense.
points.note: Accept: ~50% crashes roughly once a decade, ~20% drawdowns multiple times per decade, inevitable recurring storms wiping out all-offense managers. Do not credit: generic statements that markets are cyclical or volatile.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Launching into a crash helps in three main ways: starting point, habits, and investor base.

First, the starting point is favorable. A new fund has no legacy positions to defend, no losses to recover before earning performance fees, and no redemptions forcing it to sell. It can deploy fresh cash at depressed valuations while established managers are busy managing damage, so its early track record is built from a low base.

Second, the formative experience shapes lasting habits. A manager whose first days involve a crash internalises risk management, liquidity discipline, position sizing and scepticism about leverage. Veterans of a long bull market may have been rewarded for buying every dip and riding rising valuations, which makes it hard to separate their skill from the market's tailwind. Their instincts are untested when conditions change.

Third, capital raised in a crisis tends to be stickier. Investors who commit amid panic are usually more patient and aligned with the manager, giving a stable base.

This is a tendency, not a guarantee: many crash-era launches fail simply because raising money is hard, and survivorship bias flatters the ones we remember.

points.why: The response says veterans were rewarded for buying dips but leaves unstated whether that success leads them to expect severe crashes to reverse.
The response lists risk-management habits without explaining how starting in a crash teaches managers to revise their views or cut exposure when conditions deteriorate.
The response never links recurring major drawdowns to the cost of staying exposed through them.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Launching into a severe crash gives a new manager clean capital, intact incentives, and resilient backers at the exact moment bull-market veterans are constrained by legacy baggage. Deploying fresh cash with no prior holdings lets a newcomer buy high-quality assets at trough valuations, whereas incumbents often face panic redemptions, margin pressure, and psychological anchoring to underwater positions—turning them into forced sellers rather than opportunistic buyers.

Structurally, steep drawdowns bury veteran funds far beneath their high-water marks, eliminating performance fees for years, driving away key talent, and inducing career-risk conservatism right when offense pays most. A crash-vintage fund instead compounds from depressed prices with an unencumbered net asset value, establishing an early track record that attracts durable capital. Just as importantly, raising money amid panic filters out momentum-chasing allocators in favor of genuinely contrarian limited partners, while instilling permanent downside discipline in a manager unspoiled by decade-long bull-market habits like cheap leverage, crowded growth trades, and valuation complacency.

points.why: The response links bull-market habits to valuation complacency and anchoring but never says veterans expect severe crashes to reverse quickly.
The response claims a crash instills downside discipline but never explains that it teaches managers to change course or cut exposure when conditions deteriorate.
The response describes how steep drawdowns hurt incumbent funds but does not link recurring major drawdowns to the cost of failing to de-risk.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
A manager who launches into a crash starts buying when assets are cheap, fear is high and forced sellers are dumping good businesses. That gives them a low starting point, often strong early returns, and no losses to climb back from before earning performance fees. A track record that starts near a market bottom also compounds well and attracts investors.

The bigger edge is what the crash teaches. Liquidity can disappear, correlations jump toward one, leverage and redemptions can force selling, and clients panic. A new manager learns all of this before forming habits, so they tend to build careful risk management, position sizing and staying power into their process from the start.

Veterans who came up in a decade-long bull market may never have faced a real drawdown. Rising markets reward buying dips, crowding into momentum and using leverage, so it's easy to mistake market gains (beta) for skill (alpha). Their confidence and methods haven't been tested. When the cycle turns, those habits can cause large losses, while the crash-era manager has already been through it and knows how they react under pressure.

points.why: The response says bull markets reward buying dips but leaves unstated whether veterans carry that habit into severe crashes because they expect a rebound.
The response credits crash experience with better position sizing and staying power but gives no account of managers cutting exposure when conditions deteriorate.
The response mentions losses when the cycle turns without establishing that severe drawdowns recur often enough to punish managers who consistently stay exposed.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Launching a fund into a severe crash gives a manager three structural and psychological advantages that bull-market veterans rarely possess. First, the new manager starts with unencumbered cash at precisely the moment quality assets trade at distressed valuations. Veterans, by contrast, are often trapped managing legacy drawdowns, underwater high-water marks, and forced redemptions from panicked clients, which turns them into sellers rather than buyers. Second, a crash acts as a harsh formative filter. Managers forged in a decade-long bull market are conditioned to reward momentum, leverage, and crowded narratives, often mistaking a rising tide for skill and struggling to adapt when regimes shift. A manager baptized in a downturn internalizes liquidity risk, downside protection, and valuation discipline from day one, building habits that compound across future cycles. Finally, raising capital during a panic naturally selects for contrarian, patient limited partners, leaving the fund with a stickier, more aligned investor base when the next crisis arrives.

points.why: The response links bull-market experience to momentum chasing and difficulty adapting, without saying veterans expect severe crashes to reverse quickly.
The response says a crash teaches downside protection in general but does not explain how it trains managers to cut exposure when market conditions deteriorate.
The response anticipates future crises without explaining that major drawdowns recur with some regularity and punish funds that stay fully exposed.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A manager who launches during a crash has fresh cash when many established funds are nursing losses, meeting redemptions, or cutting risk. Forced selling can push even healthy companies to prices that imply far worse outcomes than their businesses warrant. Buying at those prices gives the new fund a low cost basis, and a recovery can give it a head start in both compounding and building a track record.

The more durable advantage is what the manager learns early. A crash makes liquidity, leverage, and position sizing immediate concerns. A decade-long bull market can reward concentrated bets, leverage, and buying every dip, making it easy to mistake a favorable market for skill. The cheap entry prices are a one-time opportunity, but the habits formed under stress can help the manager through several market cycles.

points.why: The response says bull markets reward buying dips, but it does not say veterans come to expect severe crashes to reverse quickly.
The response identifies liquidity, leverage, and position sizing as immediate concerns without saying the manager learns to cut exposure when market conditions deteriorate.
The reference to several market cycles does not establish that severe drawdowns recur regularly and punish managers who stay fully exposed.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Launching into a crash can give a manager two advantages. If the fund has fresh capital and stable investors, it can buy sound businesses at prices that already reflect deep pessimism. A veteran may recognize the same bargains but have to sell holdings to meet redemptions.

The crash can also shape the new manager’s judgment for decades. A long bull market can make leverage or a habit of buying every dip look like stock-picking skill. Managing money through a crash teaches firsthand how quickly liquidity can vanish and how to distinguish a temporary price decline from permanent damage to a business. Those lessons can help the manager take risk when prices justify it and preserve the ability to invest through the next downturn.

points.why: The response says a bull market can make dip-buying look skillful, but it does not say veterans carry that habit into severe crashes because they expect a rebound.
The response describes learning about liquidity and permanent business damage without connecting those lessons to cutting exposure when market conditions deteriorate.
The response mentions a future downturn without establishing that severe drawdowns recur regularly and punish managers who never reduce risk.
